blocks.prompt: The Mountain Made by Hand
blocks.text: About four thousand five hundred years ago, in a place called Egypt, thousands of workers began stacking stone. When they finished, they had built the Great Pyramid of Giza. It stood as tall as a forty story building, and it was made of more than two million blocks. The average block weighed more than a car. The workers had no machines. No engines, no cranes, no trucks. They cut the blocks out of the ground with copper tools and wooden wedges. They loaded each block onto a wooden sled and dragged it across the sand. Here is the clever part. A man walked in front of the sled and poured water on the sand. Wet sand is firmer than dry sand, so the sled slid along instead of sinking in. Scientists tested this and found that wet sand cuts the pulling work almost in half. For a long time people said slaves built the pyramids. They did not. Archaeologists found the workers' town right next to the pyramid, with bakeries, breweries, and a cemetery. The workers were paid in bread and beer. Their skeletons show broken bones that were set and healed, so somebody looked after them. They gave their teams proud names, like Friends of Khufu.

blocks.prompt: Four and a Half Thousand Years, and Still Standing
blocks.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built as a tomb for a pharaoh named Khufu, around 2560 BC. That is roughly forty five centuries ago. It is the oldest of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and it is the only one still standing. The numbers are hard to hold in your head. The pyramid contains about 2.3 million blocks of stone. It rose to 481 feet, and it stayed the tallest structure humans had ever made for about 3,800 years. Nothing beat it until a cathedral spire went up in England in the 1300s. What impresses engineers is not the size. It is the accuracy. The base is a square with sides about 756 feet long, and those four sides differ from each other by less than two inches. The whole base is level to within about an inch. The four faces point almost exactly at north, south, east, and west, off true north by roughly a twentieth of a degree. The builders had no compass and no laser. They almost certainly used the stars. The pyramid you see in photographs is not unfinished. It is stripped. It was once wrapped in polished white limestone, cut so precisely that the joints are thinner than a fingernail. In sunlight it would have blazed. Over the centuries people quarried that smooth skin away to build the city of Cairo, leaving the rough steps we see today. The shape helps it survive. A pyramid is nearly all base. Its weight presses down and inward onto ground that is already carrying it, so there is almost nothing for gravity to topple.

blocks.prompt: The Diary of a Man Who Hauled Stone
blocks.text: For centuries the Great Pyramid was an argument. Everyone could see it. Nobody could prove how it was built, or by whom. Into that gap poured guesses: slaves under the whip, lost civilizations, visitors from the sky. The evidence, when it finally arrived, was less dramatic and far more interesting. It was paperwork. In 2013, archaeologists digging at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbor on the Red Sea, pulled hundreds of papyrus fragments out of the sand. They turned out to be the oldest inscribed papyri ever found, and one set was a work diary. It belonged to a middle ranking official named Merer, who supervised a crew of about forty men. Merer wrote down what his crew did, day by day, in the twenty seventh year of Khufu's reign. They rowed barges up the Nile to the limestone quarries at Tura, loaded blocks, and delivered them to the building site at Giza. Round trip: a few days. Over and over. Merer's diary is a shipping log. It is also the only eyewitness account of the Great Pyramid being built, written by a man who was there. What Merer describes is not a mob of slaves. It is a workforce, organized into teams, fed and housed and paid. Excavations at Giza have filled in the rest of that picture: a workers' town with bakeries, breweries, and cattle bones by the thousand, and a cemetery where laborers were buried with care. Their skeletons carry broken bones that were set and healed. Somebody treated them. Plenty is still unknown. The loudest arguments are about ramps, because no ramp for the Great Pyramid has ever been found. A straight ramp long enough to reach the top would have needed more material than the pyramid itself. A spiral ramp would have hidden the corners the surveyors needed to sight along. One researcher proposes a ramp built inside the pyramid, corkscrewing upward within the masonry. The honest answer is that the method is not settled. That is worth sitting with. We can read the diary of a man who delivered the stone. We know what his crew ate for dinner. We know the base is level to within an inch and aimed at true north to within a twentieth of a degree. And we still cannot say for certain how the blocks went up.

2.3 million blocks at Giza
Aimed at true north within a twentieth of a degree

blocks.prompt: The Pyramid Problem
blocks.text: Start with a correction. Egypt does not have the most pyramids. Sudan does. More than two hundred of them stand in the desert at Meroe, Nuri, and El-Kurru, built by the kings and queens of Kush centuries after the Egyptian pyramid age had ended. They are steeper, smaller, and largely unvisited. Cross the Atlantic and you find pyramids again, at Teotihuacan and Chichen Itza, built by people who had never heard of Egypt and never could have. The pyramid is not one civilization's idea. It is what you get when you want to build something tall out of stone and you have no steel. Pile the material wide at the bottom, narrow it as you rise, and gravity works for you instead of against you. Every culture that tried to build high in stone arrived at roughly the same answer, because the physics offered them no other. What makes the Egyptian pyramids extraordinary is not the concept. It is the learning curve, and the fact that we can still walk around and look at it. Around 2670 BC, an official named Imhotep built the first one for King Djoser at Saqqara. It is not a true pyramid. It is six flat tombs stacked on top of each other, shrinking as they go, and it was the largest stone building anyone had yet attempted. It still stands. Then came Sneferu, Khufu's father, who built three pyramids and got the answer wrong twice. His first, at Meidum, appears to have been pushed too steep, and much of its outer structure now lies in a heap of rubble around its core. His second, at Dahshur, began at fifty four degrees and then, partway up, flinched. The builders dropped the angle to forty three degrees and finished it at that gentler slope. It is called the Bent Pyramid, and its kink is a decision, frozen in stone, made by a worried engineer roughly forty six centuries ago. Sneferu's third attempt, the Red Pyramid, was built at the safer angle from the ground up. It worked. Khufu inherited that knowledge. His pyramid at Giza is what a civilization builds once it has stopped guessing: 2.3 million blocks, a base level to within about an inch, four faces aimed at true north to within a twentieth of a degree, and a height of 481 feet that went unbeaten by any structure on Earth for roughly 3,800 years. And we still do not know how they raised the blocks. That sentence should be uncomfortable. We have the diary of Merer, an official who barged limestone to the site and logged it. We have the workers' town, its bakeries and breweries and the cattle bones of their dinners, and their graves, and their healed fractures. We know they organized into named teams. We know almost everything except the central act. No ramp for the Great Pyramid has been found, and every proposed ramp has a problem: a straight one would need more material than the pyramid, a spiral one would hide the corners the surveyors had to sight along, an internal one is ingenious and unproven. The gap invites nonsense, and it always has. Because the method is missing, people have filled the hole with lost continents and spacecraft, which is a strange insult to offer a workforce whose dinner menu we can reconstruct. The honest position is harder to sit with and more respectful. People did this. They were very good at it. The record of exactly how is simply lost. Not every silence is a mystery. Some of it is just time doing what time does.
